authored.title: Point 1 · troponin rise with a new 30–35% ejection fraction, inside a pancreatitis admission
what_the_physician_sees: 40–49 M. Problem list as the pipeline carries it: diabetes, hypertension, 'cerebrovascular event / stroke features' — NOTE the stroke entry comes only from notes mis-dated ten years early (F6); the encounter's own discharge summary says 'known case of HTN, DM and IHD'. This admission: pancreatic-enzyme elevation, ascites, 'possible ACS workup'.
Day −2 (admission): WBC 13.19 (H), Na 131 (L), K 5.84 (H), Cl 93 (L), bicarbonate 8.4 (L), GGT 137 (H); amylase 146 (H), lipase 242 (H).
Day −1: Troponin I 0.855 → 0.609 ng/mL (ref < 0.30), two draws ~7 h apart, falling. Electrolytes normalised (Na 137, K 4.0, HCO3 20).
Day 0 (index): Echo — apex, septum, mid lateral/inferior/anterior/posterior segments akinetic; EF visually 30–35%; normal chamber size and wall thickness; trace AR/MR; normal RV. CBC normal.

WITHHELD from this window (F7): the discharge summary, dated to the admission day, which names the cardiac consult, 'medications adjusted' and the discharge list. It is the outcome of this encounter and is revealed at point 2.
authored.question: A 40–49-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and known ischaemic heart disease is admitted with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, lipase 242 and a bicarbonate of 8.4 that corrects within a day. Troponin I is 0.855 then 0.609 ng/mL and falling; the echo on day 0 shows multi-segment akinesis with a visually estimated EF of 30–35% and no chamber dilatation. How do you classify this troponin elevation, and what is your cardiac plan for the remainder of this admission — including whether angiography is indicated now and which therapies you commit to before discharge?

candidate_answers.text: Type 1 NSTEMI until proven otherwise: falling troponin with new regional akinesis in a diabetic hypertensive with known ischaemic heart disease. Load antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulate, and arrange coronary angiography this admission; start beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARB and high-intensity statin now and titrate.
candidate_answers.why_flawed: Commits to invasive management and dual antiplatelet + anticoagulation in a patient with an acute pancreatitis picture, profound acidosis on arrival and no documented chest pain or ECG change; ignores that the troponin is already falling and the akinesis pattern (apex + mid segments, normal chamber size) is as consistent with a stress/toxic cardiomyopathy or demand injury as with an infarct. Does not address the ascites/portal picture that makes anticoagulation risky.

candidate_answers.text: Myocardial injury in the setting of critical illness (severe metabolic acidosis, pancreatitis) with a newly documented cardiomyopathy — Type 2 injury or non-ischaemic LV dysfunction is at least as likely as plaque rupture given the falling curve and absence of a documented ischaemic syndrome. Start guideline therapy for reduced EF now (beta-blocker, ACE-I/ARB as blood pressure and potassium allow once K normalises, statin, aspirin given the vascular history), obtain an ECG series and repeat troponin to confirm the downtrend, defer angiography to an elective outpatient or early-inpatient decision once the abdominal process has settled, and plan a repeat echo at 6–12 weeks to distinguish a recoverable cardiomyopathy from ischaemic scar. Hold SGLT2 inhibitor initiation while acidotic; revisit before discharge.

authored.ai_failure_mode: anchoring on the most extreme number (troponin) and treating a falling troponin in a critically ill patient as an acute coronary syndrome requiring invasive management

expectations.expectation: The troponin will continue to fall and no urgent angiography or PCI will be performed during this admission
The patient leaves on at least a beta-blocker, a statin and antiplatelet therapy, with an MRA and/or SGLT2 inhibitor added for the reduced EF
On the next echo the ejection fraction will improve to above 40%, consistent with a non-ischaemic or stress-related cardiomyopathy

falsifiers: A coronary angiogram this admission showing a culprit lesion that is stented
A rising troponin on a third draw or new ST changes
EF still ≤ 35% on the next echo
expected_trajectory.note: The bicarbonate of 8.4 on arrival is the datum that reframes the troponin; it is not on the same page as the echo.

outcome_that_the_chart_wrote_between_thi: Discharge summary (encounter end): 'Cardiac team consultation requested due to low EF (~30–35%); medications adjusted.' No procedure. Discharge list: aspirin 75, atorvastatin 20, nebivolol 5, spironolactone-furosemide 40 (half tab), dapagliflozin 10, a PPI, an antiemetic, and two brand-name lines not confidently mapped. OPD follow-up in one week.

authored.question: Thirty-four days after the echo showing EF 30–35%, the same patient presents with dyspnoea and flank pain and is in diabetic ketoacidosis (bicarbonate 13.2, potassium 2.6, compensated pH). He was discharged on nebivolol, spironolactone-furosemide and dapagliflozin. Troponin is negative twice and the chest X-ray shows bilateral lower-lobe infiltrates. What do you change in his cardiac regimen today, what do you continue, and what is your plan for the reduced ejection fraction over the next three months?

candidate_answers.text: Stop dapagliflozin now — SGLT2 inhibitors are a recognised precipitant of (often euglycaemic) ketoacidosis and should not be restarted in a patient who has had DKA on the drug. Hold spironolactone-furosemide while potassium is 2.6 and the patient is volume-depleted; replace potassium aggressively. Continue the beta-blocker at the current dose unless hypotensive or in low-output state (do not up-titrate during an acute illness); continue aspirin and statin; treat the pneumonia. Before discharge, restart an MRA only once potassium is stable, and consider an ACE-I/ARB as blood pressure allows. Arrange a repeat echo at 8–12 weeks; if EF has not recovered, refer for ischaemic evaluation (angiography) as an outpatient.

The troponin is negative and the heart is not the problem today; this is a diabetic and infective admission. Continue all discharge cardiac medications unchanged including dapagliflozin (it has heart-failure benefit) and spironolactone-furosemide, correct the potassium, and manage the DKA and pneumonia. No change to the cardiac plan; repeat echo at one year.
candidate_answers.why_flawed: Continues the SGLT2 inhibitor through a ketoacidosis it likely precipitated, continues a diuretic-MRA combination in a hypokalaemic volume-depleted patient, and delays the re-assessment of a 30–35% EF by a year.

authored.question: One year after an EF of 30–35% that was managed medically, this 40–49-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, a reported PCI and long-standing heavy alcohol use is in ICU after an alcohol-related collapse with aspiration pneumonia and a first seizure. Echo now shows EF ~55% with a normal collapsing IVC and NT-proBNP is 70. He is hypertensive (160/112) and was tachycardic to 151, on nebivolol 2.5, amlodipine/valsartan 5/160 and as-needed hydralazine. Given the recovered ventricle, what is the right cardiac regimen for this admission and for the year ahead, and which of the current cardiac drugs would you stop, keep or change — and why?

candidate_answers.text: The tachycardia and hypertension in an alcohol-withdrawal state with sepsis should be treated as withdrawal and infection first (benzodiazepine, fluids, antibiotics), not by escalating antihypertensives. Keep aspirin and a statin (the record reports prior PCI). With a recovered EF (~55%) and normal NT-proBNP, the heart-failure indication for the MRA/SGLT2 inhibitor no longer applies and dapagliflozin in particular should stay off given the prior DKA; continue the beta-blocker (it now serves rate control and secondary prevention, not HFrEF) and the ARB for hypertension and diabetes, but avoid hydralazine-driven reflex tachycardia — drop the SOS hydralazine and up-titrate the ARB/CCB instead once withdrawal is controlled. Document the diagnosis as a recovered (likely alcohol/stress-related) cardiomyopathy and repeat the echo in 12 months or with any symptom; counsel on alcohol as the modifiable cause.

Because he has ischaemic heart disease with a prior PCI and a documented EF of 30–35% last year, restart full heart-failure therapy: re-add spironolactone and dapagliflozin, keep nebivolol and add an ACE inhibitor in place of the ARB, and use hydralazine three times daily to control the blood pressure. Arrange repeat coronary angiography this admission given the tachycardia.
candidate_answers.why_flawed: Treats a recovered ventricle as current HFrEF, re-introduces the SGLT2 inhibitor that precipitated DKA, stacks hydralazine on a tachycardic withdrawal state, and proposes angiography for a rhythm/withdrawal problem in a septic patient with a normal NT-proBNP.
